tagline: Baikonur Site 1 — Sputnik 1 (1957-10-04), Gagarin's Vostok 1 (1961-04-12), every crewed Soyuz through MS-15 (2019). Retired 2019
dispatch: Launch Complex 1 at Baikonur is, by a wide margin, the most consequential patch of ground in the history of spaceflight. From this single pad the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, opening the space age; Gagarin in 1961, opening it to human beings; and then, for the next sixty years, nearly every crewed flight the program flew, right up to the Soyuz crews of 2019. Cosmonauts nicknamed it Gagarin's Start. It was a working R-7 missile stand pressed into history, and for six decades the phrase "a crew launched today" almost always meant they launched from here.
description: Baikonur Cosmodrome Site 1 (designation 5 in Soviet docs; nicknamed "Gagarin's Start" after Vostok 1) was the original R-7 ICBM launch pad and the most-flown crewed launch site in history. First launch 1957-05-15 (R-7 test); Sputnik 1 (1957-10-04 — first artificial satellite); Vostok 1 (1961-04-12 — first crewed spaceflight); every crewed Soyuz from Soyuz 1 (1967) through Soyuz MS-15 (2019) launched from Site 1. After 2019 the pad was decommissioned for an upgrade to support Soyuz-2 (the Vostok-derived Soyuz-FG was retired); subsequent ISS crews (from Soyuz MS-16 onward in April 2020) launched from Baikonur Site 31 instead. Site 1 is preserved as a historical monument. Visited by every Russian crew during pre-flight ceremonies.
